name: L-Tryptophan
lead: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that humans cannot make and must obtain from protein foods such as meat, dairy, eggs, nuts and seeds. Besides building proteins it is a precursor of serotonin, melatonin and niacin [1]. Frederick Hopkins first isolated it in 1901 from casein [1].

In looks-oriented circles it sits in the recovery category. People take it as a supplement aiming at deeper, more consolidated sleep and steadier mood, on the reasoning that better-rested people train harder, recover more fully and tend to look fresher. That is a chain rather than a direct effect: tryptophan -> serotonin and melatonin precursor -> sleep and mood -> recovery and training consistency.

Research on the supplement itself is mostly about sleep and mood. A 2022 meta-analysis of sleep trials found shorter wake time after sleep onset with supplementation, and a 2021 systematic review of eleven randomized trials reported that several showed lower anxiety and higher positive mood in healthy adults [6][7]. Wikipedia describes the older depression evidence as weak, with a 2001 Cochrane review finding two eligible studies, and notes the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline advises against it for insomnia [1]. In 1989 supplements were linked to an outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) [1].
infobox: Over-the-counter supplement in US and UK; prescription in some European countries [1]

paras: Supplement users describe tryptophan as an evening aid for falling and staying asleep, and some combine it with other recovery supplements. The appearance rationale runs through a chain: sleep affects training adaptation, and mood affects diet and routine adherence, so better sleep and steadier mood are expected to support training and a rested look. Dietary tryptophan from protein foods is the ordinary way intake is maintained; the nutrition trials below study requirements and absorption from foods such as maize [1][5].
Marketed for temporary relief of anxiety, mood swings and sleeplessness; one US product label lists these uses [2]. In some European countries it is available by prescription [1].

Over 95% of tryptophan is broken down through the kynurenine pathway; smaller amounts become serotonin and, from it, melatonin [1]. Gut microbes also transform tryptophan into metabolites such as indoles that interact with host immune receptors [3][4]. Reviews of tryptophan metabolism also describe its role in immune regulation and in cancer and neurodegeneration research [8]. Because serotonin made in the brain depends on tryptophan crossing the blood-brain barrier alongside other amino acids, researchers studying mood have also used tryptophan depletion experiments, including in obsessive-compulsive patients [9].

sections.h: Dietary sources and the serotonin pathway
paras: Tryptophan reaches the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier competing with other large neutral amino acids, which is why researchers have used both depletion and loading designs to examine serotonin-related mood effects [9][7]. Gut bacteria convert part of dietary tryptophan into indole derivatives that can activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and influence mucosal immunity [3][4][15]. A 2019 Physiological Reviews article places tryptophan metabolites within the wider microbiota-gut-brain axis [16].

The serotonin-theory umbrella review matters to how the supplement is framed: the authors reported that the literature does not support a simple low-serotonin explanation of depression [11], so the case for tryptophan as a mood aid rests mainly on the small supplementation trials in healthy adults [7].

Reported effects include nausea, diarrhea, drowsiness, lightheadedness, headache, dry mouth and blurred vision, and combination with MAOIs or SSRIs can cause serotonin syndrome [1]. The US drug label for one product advises pregnant or breastfeeding users to consult a professional [2].

Commercial tryptophan is made by fermenting serine and indole with engineered bacteria such as E. coli [1]. In research, acute tryptophan depletion is used to study mood and behaviour, and tryptophan is used as a natural fluorescent probe for studying proteins [1].

sections.h: Dietary sources and the turkey belief
paras: Tryptophan is found in most proteins, with high amounts in eggs, soy, cheese and seeds, and turkey contains about the same as other poultry and meats [1]. The 2002 US Institute of Medicine set the adult recommended allowance at 5 mg per kg of body weight per day [1]. Wikipedia describes the common belief that turkey causes sleepiness as largely unsupported and attributes post-meal drowsiness more plausibly to carbohydrate-rich foods eaten alongside it, which change how amino acids reach the brain [1].

More than 1,500 US cases of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome and at least 37 deaths were reported, linked to tryptophan supplements, which the FDA recalled in 1989 and largely barred from public sale in 1990 [1]. Later studies traced the outbreak to contaminated batches from one Japanese manufacturer, though some researchers suspect tryptophan itself may contribute [1]. The FDA eased restrictions in 2001 and maintained import limits until 2005 [1].

The first case was reported to the CDC in November 1989, and some cases may have occurred two to three years earlier [22]. Investigators linked the outbreak to batches made by Showa Denko, produced by a bacterium grown at one of its plants; of 63 trace contaminants identified, six were associated with the syndrome, and no single impurity has been firmly established as the cause [22]. The manufacturer had recently changed its process, including reduced use of activated charcoal, skipped filtration in some batches and a genetically engineered bacterial strain, and these overlapping changes could not be separated [22]. Wikipedia notes that tryptophan itself may contribute, since some EMS cases occurred without tryptophan exposure [22].

Symptoms in the acute phase include severe muscle pain, breathlessness, fever, fatigue, joint pain and swelling, and numbness or tingling in the limbs; a chronic phase can involve eosinophilic fasciitis and nerve and muscle problems [22]. Treatment involves stopping tryptophan products and giving glucocorticoids, and most patients recover fully or stabilise [22]. After the 1990 sales ban, 5-HTP became a popular substitute supplement [22].

sections.h: Use in recovery and training communities
paras: On T Nation, tryptophan appears mainly in bedtime supplement lists. Posters in training logs describe combining it with magnesium glycinate and low-dose melatonin to help with sleep during periods of poor recovery, for instance while recovering on testosterone replacement therapy [17][18]. Another poster remarks that sleeping through the night is anabolic and cites tryptophan in celery as one of several compounds that may aid rest [19]. Some posters report that over-the-counter calming supplements including tryptophan did little for them [20]. Dietary tryptophan from turkey, nuts and seeds is also mentioned in discussions of serotonin and mood [21].

Sleep: a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis (18 articles collected, 4 pooled) found that tryptophan supplementation shortened wake after sleep onset, with the authors reporting a larger effect at 1 g or more per day, and no effect on other sleep components [6]. A 2025 meta-analysis of 28 randomized trials of dietary supplement interventions found improvements in several sleep measures across supplements generally [10].

Mood: a 2021 systematic review identified 11 randomized trials in healthy adults; four showed significant differences versus control on negative or happy feelings, and the authors concluded tryptophan may lower anxiety and raise positive mood, with no effect on aggressive feelings [7]. A 2023 umbrella review of the serotonin theory of depression concluded that evidence does not support a simple serotonin deficit explanation of depression, which bears on how the supplement's rationale is interpreted [11].

Older and other findings: the 2001 Cochrane review of tryptophan for depression found two eligible studies (64 participants) and insufficient evidence, and the 2017 AASM guideline advises against it for insomnia [1]. Registered trials are mostly nutritional: tryptophan requirements in adults and children [5][12], absorption from foods [13], and dietary tryptophan and aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation [14]. No studies found that test it for appearance outcomes.

lore.intro: Among lifters, tryptophan is discussed as one part of a bedtime routine rather than as a stand-alone supplement [17][18].

claims.claim: Tryptophan at bedtime improves sleep and therefore recovery
claims.believers: Training-log posters list it with magnesium and melatonin as what helped them sleep better, and say better sleep supports recovery [17][18][19].
claims.experts: A 2022 meta-analysis found shorter wake after sleep onset with supplementation and no effect on other sleep components, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline advises against it for insomnia [6][1].

claims.claim: Tryptophan lifts mood and lowers anxiety
claims.believers: Users take it for mood and calm, linking tryptophan intake to serotonin [21].
claims.experts: A 2021 systematic review of 11 trials in healthy adults found four with significant differences on negative or happy feelings and concluded it may lower anxiety and raise positive mood [7]; a 2001 Cochrane review for depression found insufficient evidence [1].

claims.claim: Tryptophan supplements are risky because of the 1989 outbreak
claims.believers: Some posters and writers recall the outbreak when discussing amino-acid supplements.
claims.experts: More than 1,500 US cases of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome were linked to contaminated batches from one manufacturer; the FDA eased restrictions in 2001 [1]. Combination with SSRIs or MAOIs can cause serotonin syndrome [1].

claims.claim: Turkey makes you sleepy because of its tryptophan.
claims.believers: A widely repeated belief links a turkey meal to drowsiness through tryptophan and serotonin.
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes turkey has about the same tryptophan as other poultry and meats and attributes post-meal drowsiness more plausibly to the accompanying carbohydrates [1].

claims.claim: 5-HTP is a way around the tryptophan ban and does the same job.
claims.believers: After the 1990 sales ban, 5-HTP became a popular substitute supplement for people seeking the same sleep and mood support [22].
claims.experts: The EMS literature concerns tryptophan batches; no published trials have compared the two for sleep or appearance outcomes.

card.summary: An essential amino acid sold for sleep and mood; evidence is limited and a 1989 contamination outbreak shaped its regulation.
card.note: Serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs/MAOIs; 1989 EMS outbreak linked to contaminated batches.

quick.overview:
Tryptophan is an essential amino acid found in protein foods and the starting material for serotonin and melatonin. It is sold as a sleep and mood supplement.

Wikipedia cites a 2001 Cochrane review finding insufficient evidence and a 2017 sleep-medicine guideline advising against use for insomnia. No study found tests appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Most is metabolised via the kynurenine pathway; a smaller share becomes serotonin and melatonin.
quick.risks: Side effects include nausea, drowsiness and headache; combining with SSRIs or MAOIs can cause serotonin syndrome. A 1989 outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, traced largely to contaminated batches, led to US restrictions lifted in 2001.

chain: Amino acid supplies serotonin and melatonin synthesis
angle.text: People use tryptophan to support sleep and mood, which they connect to better recovery, training and a rested appearance. Studies measure sleep and mood outcomes, not appearance.
